Cartography has always been an argument about what deserves to be shown. A map that recorded everything would be the size of the territory and no use to anyone, so every map is a series of decisions about omission, and those decisions carry the mapmaker's priorities whether or not they are stated. Roads appear because someone intends to travel; contour lines appear because someone intends to climb or to farm or to shell. The convention that a map is a neutral record survives mainly because its omissions are invisible to the reader, who cannot miss what was never drawn.

Materials fail in two quite different ways and the distinction matters more than the failure. Ductile failure gives warning: the metal stretches, thins, and deforms long before it parts, and an inspector walking past has a chance of noticing. Brittle failure gives none. A crack propagates faster than the eye follows and the structure is in two pieces before anyone has registered a sound. This is why engineers will often accept a weaker material that yields gracefully over a stronger one that shatters, and why temperature matters so much: steel that is ductile in summer can be brittle on a cold morning.
